Fray
frā
v. (to frighten away; to scare off — the older sense preserved in afraid)
From Old French effrayer, to frighten; the same root that gives afraid. In the Authorized Version fray always means to scare a thing away, and twice the horror is that nobody is left alive to do it.

Biblical Definition

The word's first two uses are among the bleakest sentences in Scripture, and the bleakness is in what is not happening. In the covenant curses of Deuteronomy: “thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away” (Deu 28:26). Jeremiah repeats it over Jerusalem: “the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and none shall fray them away” (Jer 7:33). To be unburied was a disgrace in the ancient world, and to have no one even to wave the birds off is the picture of a society emptied out — no mourners, no family, no survivors. That is what the curse means. Against it stands Zechariah's night vision, where the word turns and becomes hope. The prophet sees four horns that scattered Judah, “so that no man did lift up his head”, and then four carpenters: “these are come to fray them, to cast out the horns of the Gentiles, which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah to scatter it” (Zec 1:21). The scatterers are themselves frightened away. God raises craftsmen against horns, and the people who could not lift up their heads are the ones He is defending.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fray as to fright, to terrify; and notes that in this sense it is nearly obsolete, being superseded by afraid and affray.

expand to see more

FRAY, v.t. To fright; to terrify.

1. To rub; to fret, as cloth by wearing.

FRAY, n. A broil, quarrel or violent riot.

AFRAID, pp. Impressed with fear; fearful. It is followed by of.

Key Scripture

Zec 1:21 — "Then said I, What come these to do? And he spake, saying, These are the horns which have scattered Judah, so that no man did lift up his head: but these are come to fray them, to cast out the horns of the Gentiles, which lifted up their horn over the land of Judah to scatter it."

Deu 28:26 — "And thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air, and unto the beasts of the earth, and no man shall fray them away."

Jer 7:33 — "And the carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth; and none shall fray them away."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb has simply fallen out of use in this sense; a modern reader meets fray and thinks of a quarrel or of a worn edge, and misses that Deuteronomy 28:26 is describing carrion birds nobody drives off.

The principle to recover is that God raises instruments against the instruments of judgment. Zechariah 1 shows the prophet four horns — the powers that had gored and scattered Judah until no man could lift up his head — and then, without explanation, four carpenters, whose whole business is to fray the horns away. The vision is given to a discouraged remnant working on a half-built temple. It says that the same God who permitted the scattering has already appointed the men who will end it, and that He does it with craftsmen rather than with horns of His own. What frightens the powers of the earth is not a bigger horn but a workman sent by God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew charad (H2729), to tremble, and causatively to make afraid; qeren (H7161), a horn; charash (H2796), a craftsman, a carpenter.

expand to see more

Hebrew charad (H2729) — to tremble, and in the causative to terrify, to drive away by frightening; Deuteronomy 28:26, Jeremiah 7:33, Zechariah 1:21.

Hebrew qeren (H7161) — a horn, the standing symbol of power; the four horns that scattered Judah.

Hebrew charash (H2796) — an engraver, craftsman, carpenter, smith; the four whom God raised against the horns.

Hebrew zarah (H2219) — to scatter, to winnow; what the horns had done to Judah.

Hebrew nebelah (H5038) — a carcase, a corpse; what the fowls were left undisturbed upon.

Usage

"“No man shall fray them away” — and that is the curse."

"“None shall fray them away” — Jeremiah, over Jerusalem."

"“These are come to fray them” — four carpenters against four horns."
